cards.back: Which stored vectors are nearest to this query vector, among those that pass my filters?

cards.front: Why store metadata with each vector
cards.back: One record per chunk; the metadata is what makes filtered search and deletes possible.

cards.front: When exact search stops being enough
cards.back: Exact search is fine up to roughly a million vectors. Beyond that, systems use an approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) index.
By recall: how often the true nearest neighbours appear in the results. ANN trades a little recall for orders of magnitude less work.
A layered graph: search starts at the top with long hops and drops a layer each time no neighbour is closer. High recall and low latency, but memory-hungry because the graph lives in RAM.
Clusters the vectors and searches only the probed clusters. Smaller and simpler, but needs training on a sample and recall depends on how many clusters you probe.
How many IVF clusters are searched. More probes means better recall and slower queries.
Compresses vectors 8 to 32 times at some loss of accuracy, usually paired with a rerank on the full vectors.

cards.front: Post-filter vs pre-filter vs filtered ANN
cards.back: Post-filter can leave almost nothing; pre-filter is accurate but slow when many survive; filtered ANN skips non-matching vectors during traversal and is what you want for permissions.
memory ≈ vectors × dimensions × 4 bytes × 1.3 to 2 for index overhead. 50M × 768 dims ≈ 154 GB raw, roughly 200 to 300 GB with HNSW.

cards.front: A good default vector store answer
cards.back: Start with the database the team already operates if it supports filtered vector search. Move to a dedicated engine when scale or latency demands it.

quiz.q: Around what size do systems usually switch from exact search to an ANN index?
quiz.why: Exact search is fine up to roughly a million vectors; beyond that ANN indexes are used.

quiz.q: What is the main cost of an HNSW index?
choices: Memory, because the graph lives in RAM
It needs training on a sample first
It compresses vectors and loses accuracy
quiz.why: HNSW gives high recall and low latency but is memory-hungry.

quiz.q: In an IVF index, what happens when you raise nprobe?
choices: Recall goes down and queries get faster
Recall goes up and queries get slower
quiz.why: Probing more clusters finds more true neighbours but does more work.

quiz.q: A permission filter matches only 1% of chunks. Which approach can return almost nothing?
quiz.why: Post-filtering searches first, so a selective filter drops most of the top results.

quiz.q: Roughly how much raw vector memory do 50M chunks at 768 dimensions in float32 need?
Your team already runs Postgres and has a few million vectors that need transactions with other data. What fits?
choices: A dedicated engine on day one
No vector store; use exact search in the app
quiz.why: pgvector suits teams already on Postgres needing transactions, up to tens of millions of vectors.

quiz.q: What does product quantisation trade away?
choices: Some accuracy, for 8 to 32 times smaller vectors
quiz.why: PQ compresses vectors and loses some accuracy, so it is often paired with a rerank on full vectors.
